newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says will succceed in pushing through reform.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says will succceed in pushing through reform.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, facing mounting criticism over his failure to steer far-reaching reforms through his coalition, defended his record on Saturday and said he would succeed in the end.

Kohl told the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily that some of his critics were out to capitalise on the deadlock in his ruling coalition over planned tax and pension reforms and appealed to his detractors to be "fair" on him.

"The whole country's survival depends on our success in pushing through these reforms," the 66-year-old chancellor said in an interview with the paper, after a week of intense media speculation over whether it was time for him to step down.

"I am absolutely convinced I will be successful in doing my part to push them (reforms) through and even when the tide is against me, I will not be deterred," he said, adding that he had solved seemingly insurmountable problems in the past.
"As already announced, I will make my decision known as to whether I will stand again as chancellor in the 1998 general election when I consider the time to be right," he said.

Kohl's failure to push tax and pension reform plans smoothly through the coalition, added to the blow of record unemployment, has caused disquiet among his Christian Democrats (CDU) and fuelled media speculation over his future.

One opposition leader dubbed the situation "twilight of the chancellor", the press has run headlines such as "Autumn of the Patriarch" and Kohl's indecision over whether to stand again in general elections next year has compounded the sense of drift.

Kohl conceded he was not above criticism: "But it just annoys me when criticism is not what it says it's about, when people just want to increase their status by it. Helmut Kohl also deserves a minimum quota of fairness too."

Kohl firmed his resolve to achieve his government's goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000: "It is the joint duty of industry, trade unions and politicians. When we act resolutely we can achieve this goal or come pretty close to it."

He said his enthusiasm for European integration did not mean he would tolerate any weakening of the Maastricht criteria for European monetary union (EMU) and sought to quell German fears about swapping a strong mark for a weaker euro.

"I warn against misunderstanding my commitment to Europe along the lines of 'Kohl is so enthusiastic about Europe that he'll go soft on the stability criteria at the end'," he said, vowing to guard the Germany currency's tradition of stability.

"Anyone who is ready to introduce the euro in place of the mark, as I am, knows that the Germans' experience with the mark is one of the best in history and that we will not give up this accomplishment in the future," the chancellor said.
Kohl's remarks came a week after he gave his strongest hint yet he was seriously thinking of retiring in an interview on French television.
He said he might decide on this after the European Union's Maastricht Treaty reform summit in Amsterdam in June.
Earlier this week the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zietung warned Kohl it did not do to look like a ditherer:
"Kohl is no longer the unchallenged master of what happens. If he doesn't want the twilight of the chancellor to become a polar night, he must make up his mind on 1998 soon."
